draft.title: Where a line meets a parabola
card: Where a line meets a parabola, both give the same \(y\) for the same \(x\). So set the two rules equal, rearrange to \(= 0\) and solve.
Example: \(y = x^{2} - 2x - 3\) and \(y = x + 1\). Then \(x^{2} - 2x - 3 = x + 1\), which gives \(x^{2} - 3x - 4 = 0\). Factorising gives \((x - 4)(x + 1) = 0\), so \(x = 4\) or \(x = -1\).
Each solution is an \(x\) value. Put it into the line to find \(y\): \(x = 4\) gives \(y = 5\), and \(x = -1\) gives \(y = 0\). The graphs meet at \((4, 5)\) and \((-1, 0)\).
The number of solutions is the number of meeting points. Two solutions mean two points. One repeated solution means the line just touches the parabola. No solutions mean the line misses it.

3.alt: The parabola \(y = x^{2} - 2x - 3\), concave up with vertex \((1, -4)\), and the line \(y = x + 1\). They cross at \((-1, 0)\) and \((4, 5)\).

draft.remember: Set the line equal to the parabola, solve for \(x\), then find \(y\) from the line.

a.q: Which equation do you solve to find where \(y = x^{2} + x - 2\) meets \(y = 2x + 4\)?
a.why: Set \(x^{2} + x - 2 = 2x + 4\). Subtract \(2x\) and \(4\) from both sides to get \(x^{2} - x - 6 = 0\). Adding \(2x\) instead of subtracting it gives the tempting \(x^{2} + 3x + 2 = 0\).
a.clue: Make the two rules equal, then move everything to one side.

b.q: How many points do the line \(y = 2x - 1\) and the parabola \(y = x^{2}\) share?
opts: One point, where the line just touches
Two points, because the equation is quadratic
No points, because the line misses
b.why: Set \(x^{2} = 2x - 1\), so \(x^{2} - 2x + 1 = 0\), which is \((x - 1)^{2} = 0\). The only solution is \(x = 1\), giving the single point \((1, 1)\). A quadratic equation can have one repeated solution, so it does not always mean two points.
b.clue: Factorise and count the different values of \(x\).
